---
title: "Restrictions imposed by a fixed order"
subtitle: "3.6 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 25, three-unit law"
description: "When grades that follow the posterior means miss a lower-risk report."
---

In this three-unit posterior, unit A has the largest posterior mean from a rare high-value state while B ranks first
most often, so requiring grades to follow the mean order can miss the lowest-risk report.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Mean order: τ .25.** At two stated pairs, the mean-order boundary expects 7/10 wrong directions against 3/10 across all orders; the best mean-order cut withholds all pairs at risk .250 while placing B above A and C reaches .183.
- **Expected ranks: τ .25.** Switching to expected ranks orders the units B, C, A and recovers risk .183.
- **Equal risk: τ .30.** Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2 tie at the minimum risk, stating two and three pairs respectively.
- **Mean order: τ .50.** Mean-order cuts have risk .400 against .200 for the unrestricted optimum.
- **Mean order: τ .10.** Both methods withhold every pair at risk .100; the imposed order misses only above the cost where disclosure first pays.

<details>
<summary>Numerical illustrations and notes</summary>

The result depends on the two states and their probabilities. The cut method searches every allowed boundary
within one order, whereas the joint benchmark searches every report that meets the cap. A different cap changes
which reports enter the comparison. Each point on the curve compares the two methods at a common cost.

</details>

Standalone: [order-misses](../../embed/order-misses.html), for example `?order=rank&tau=.25`.
